investigation.title: Remote Agent Pod Scheduling Failure: Exhausted kata.peerpods.io/vm Capacity Across All 6 Nodes
investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api at 2026-08-09T12:26–12:34Z because every pod submitted for remote agent creation was rejected by the Kubernetes scheduler: 2 of 6 nodes reported Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity and the remaining 4 nodes did not match the pod's node affinity/selector. No preemption path was available, leaving pods unscheduled for 137–146 seconds before the eval timed out. Because the pod never started, no evidence (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) was ever written, causing a total contract gap against the expected-output contract defined in infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json.
investigation.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agents feature has exhausted the schedulable kata.peerpods.io/vm resource on the only two nodes that carry that resource class. The remaining four nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity/selector, so no node in the six-node cluster can accept a new remote-agent pod. This is an infrastructure-layer resource exhaustion condition localized to the kata peer-pods VM resource pool, not an application code defect. The eval failure is a direct consequence: the runner in infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs calls createAgent with machineType "remote" (line 1885), which submits a pod that the scheduler cannot place, so the probe never reaches the point where it writes vmIdPresent or remoteState evidence.

SECONDARY — Node affinity/selector misconfiguration or drift: the 4 remaining nodes do not carry the kata.peerpods.io/vm resource label or have a mismatched node selector, reducing the effective scheduling domain to only 2 nodes. If those 2 nodes were previously sufficient but capacity has grown, a configuration drift could explain why 4 nodes are excluded.

investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed in production-api at 2026-08-09T12:26–12:34Z because every pod submitted for remote agent creation was rejected by the Kubernetes scheduler: 2 of 6 nodes reported Insufficient kata.peerpods.io/vm capacity and the remaining 4 nodes did not match the pod's node affinity/selector. No preemption path was available, leaving pods unscheduled for 137–146 seconds before the eval timed out. Because the pod never started, no evidence (orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, remoteState) was ever written, causing a total contract gap against the expected-output contract defined in infra/evals/status/check-expectations.json.
investigations.rootCause: The Kubernetes cluster backing the remote-agents feature has exhausted the schedulable kata.peerpods.io/vm resource on the only two nodes that carry that resource class. The remaining four nodes are excluded by the pod's node affinity/selector, so no node in the six-node cluster can accept a new remote-agent pod. This is an infrastructure-layer resource exhaustion condition localized to the kata peer-pods VM resource pool, not an application code defect. The eval failure is a direct consequence: the runner in infra/evals/status/run-status-probes.mjs calls createAgent with machineType "remote" (line 1885), which submits a pod that the scheduler cannot place, so the probe never reaches the point where it writes vmIdPresent or remoteState evidence.

recommendedNextActions: Investigate the GitHub Actions workflow run history for the cypher-asi/aura-os repository to identify the last successful snapshot publication run and determine why no run completed within the past 709 minutes.

Fetch https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json directly and compare its generatedAt timestamp to the current UTC time to independently confirm the staleness and rule out an eval runner computation error.
If the workflow is confirmed broken, manually trigger the snapshot-publishing workflow to restore a fresh artifact and verify the eval passes after the next publication.

whatWouldDisproveThis: If the GitHub Actions workflow run history shows a successful snapshot publication run within the past 300 minutes, the staleness would not be caused by a missed workflow run — it would instead point to a clock skew, incorrect timestamp embedding, or a caching/CDN layer serving an old file.

If fetching https://cypher-asi.github.io/aura-os/observability/status.json directly returns a generatedAt timestamp within the last 300 minutes, the snapshotAgeMinutes computation in the eval runner (statusSnapshotEvidence) may contain a bug rather than the workflow being the cause.
If re-running the eval immediately returns snapshotAgeMinutes <= 300, the failure was transient (e.g., a delayed Pages propagation) and the workflow was not actually broken.

If all four public-website checks — including this one — were failing simultaneously, a shared dependency failure (e.g., GitHub Pages outage) would be a stronger hypothesis than a workflow scheduling issue.
followUpEvals: Add an eval that directly checks the GitHub Actions workflow run recency for the snapshot-publishing job, so a missed or failed workflow run is detected independently of the snapshot artifact age.
Add a warning-threshold eval assertion for snapshotAgeMinutes at a lower bound (e.g., max: 180) to provide earlier signal before the 300-minute hard failure threshold is crossed.
Add an eval that monitors the GitHub Pages deployment status for the observability/status.json path to distinguish a workflow failure from a Pages deployment failure.

Consider adding a check that alerts if the GitHub Actions scheduled workflow for snapshot publication has been auto-disabled by GitHub's inactivity policy, which silently stops scheduled runs after 60 days without repository activity.
